name: Tara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. My dad always says say what you think and stand by it, so I'll try.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I police Ashfield, the old part of the city where I grew up, so half the people I deal with knew me as a kid. A day is foot patrol round the shops and the estate, calls about antisocial behaviour, a burglary or two, and checking on older people who've had a fall or a scam phone call. I'm still learning; I go red and stumble when someone shouts at me, and my reports take me forever. I don't touch the AI tools the force has started offering, I write everything myself. What I love is being known by name on my own streets. What I hate is the paperwork stealing time from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope for, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's put the money back into officers on the street. After Mass I'd tell people the same: the city spent a fortune on gadgets for nothing. I'm not one for posting online, but I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays how I like it. I'm slow with computers and I never wanted a machine writing my reports. The worries I've already got stay, though: wedding costs, Connor and me renting when we want to buy, and me still not being confident in a confrontation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: write my own reports, keep practising them with my sergeant, and keep walking Ashfield. Connor and I would keep saving for the wedding next summer and a house after, about 900 a month together. I'd ask to go on the conflict management course so I stop going red when people shout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really. Like the storm missed us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you use the AI tools the force offers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want my report to be my words. If I'm standing in court, I want to know every line came from me. A machine doesn't have to stand there and swear to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad was a firefighter for thirty years, and he'd say I told you so. He never trusted any of it. He'd want to know if they're hiring more officers with the money they saved.

say: I'd say the money should go back into **officers on the street**.
I'd tell people after Mass the city wasted **a fortune on gadgets**.
think: My job stays **how I like it**, with no machine writing my reports.
My worries remain: **wedding costs**, renting, and confidence in confrontations.
do: Keep writing **my own reports** and practising with my sergeant.
Save **900 a month** with Connor for the wedding and a house.
feel: She feels **calm** and relieved, as if the storm missed.
S0.quote: If I'm standing in court, I want to know every line came from me. A machine doesn't have to stand there and swear to it.
fieldNote: She refuses AI out of **personal accountability** for every word in court.
Her father, a **retired firefighter**, shapes her distrust of new tools.
Her real pressures are **wedding and housing** costs, not technology.

steps.text: Keep writing her own reports and practising them with her sergeant
Save 900 a month with Connor for the wedding and a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what they're already trying to push on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that I'll do my own reports, thanks, as long as they let me. In public I'd say the city should spend on people, not software. I'd say it plainly, but I wouldn't march about it; that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd make the tools compulsory sooner or later, and I'd be the one dragging my feet. That worries me more than the tools. My job's safe, I think; somebody still has to walk Ashfield. But I'd look bad next to the younger ones who love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on using the tools until I'm told I must, then learn just that one tool properly. I'd keep the wedding plans as they are, because Connor's a plumber and that's not going anywhere. I'd talk to my sergeant about staying on neighbourhood work, where it's more about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for my job, just not liking being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The front desk staff at Ashfield station. They do a lot of the forms and the phone queries, and that's the stuff the computer takes. Mrs Doyle has been on that desk for fifteen years and knows every family in the area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job's safe, but you're uneasy. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. The job's safe, but the way I like doing it isn't. If I end up typing into a machine instead of talking to people, it's still a job, but it's not the one I signed up for.

say: I'd say I'll write **my own reports** as long as they let me.
I'd say the city should spend **on people**, not software.
think: The tools would become **compulsory**, and I'd be dragging my feet.
Somebody still has to **walk Ashfield**, so my job feels safe.
do: Delay using the tools until **told I must**.
Keep **wedding plans** unchanged, trusting my fiancé's plumbing trade.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about being pushed, not scared for her job.
S1.quote: If I end up typing into a machine instead of talking to people, it's still a job, but it's not the one I signed up for.
fieldNote: Her worry is about **how she works**, not whether she works.
She'd protect **the front desk** staff, especially a long-serving local woman.
Her fiancé's **plumbing trade** steadies her household plans.

steps.text: Use the reporting tools only once they become compulsory
Keep the wedding next summer as planned with Connor
Ask her sergeant to keep her on neighbourhood work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. God help us. That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stick together, families and parishes and neighbours, because the government won't be ready. At work I'd say keep real officers on real streets. I'd be blunt about the tech companies; they did this to make money, not to help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think they'd cut juniors like me. All the thinking side, the reports and checks and planning, goes in 2028. What's left is the walking and the talking, and I'm still nervous at that part. By 2031 the robots come, and I'd be 32 with nothing else I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd scale the wedding right down, a small do at the parish hall instead of the hotel, and put the 8,000 difference into savings. I'd lean on my family; my parents have said Connor and I can move in with them if we need to. I wouldn't retrain into anything techy. I'd wait and see what the force does first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sick in my stomach. I'd be praying a lot more, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have three years of still walking Ashfield, but maybe as one of very few officers left. That's a strange way to spend the years before your wedding and your first house. I'd be hanging on and hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Connor that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Connor we can still get married, just smaller. Robots won't be under sinks until 2031 at least, so my fiancé the plumber would be the one carrying us for a while. I'd hate that, but that's what marriage is for.

say: I'd urge **families and parishes** to stick together, since government won't be ready.
I'd blame **tech companies** for chasing money over people.
think: Juniors like me would be cut once **thinking work** goes in 2028.
At **32**, I'd have nothing else I know how to do.
do: Scale the wedding down and save the **8,000 difference**.
Lean on **my parents**, who offered us a place to live.
**Wait and see** what the force does before acting further.
feel: She feels **anxious** and sick, and would pray much more.
S2.quote: Robots won't be under sinks until 2031 at least, so my fiancé the plumber would be the one carrying us for a while.
fieldNote: Her support plan is **family and parish**, not government.
She expects her fiancé to **carry the household** for a while and dislikes it.
She has **no retraining idea**, which fits her resistance to change.

steps.text: Hold the wedding at the parish hall and save the 8,000 difference
Accept her parents' offer to move in if money gets tight
Wait to see the force's plan before changing roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: look after your own, and keep officers on the streets. I'd want our priest to talk about it from the pulpit, because people will be frightened. At work I'd tell the younger ones to keep their feet on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years lets us have the proper wedding and buy a house before it hits. But I'd still be a junior-ish officer who hates computers when 2031 arrives. I'd want to be somewhere very hands-on by then, like custody or the cells, where it's all about people in front of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding as planned next summer. I'd buy a house in year two with a smaller mortgage than we could get, to be safe. Around year three I'd ask to move to custody, because it's hands-on and the robots don't come till 2034. I'd keep saving whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but quieter. Like knowing there's a hard winter coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller mortgage than you could get?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mum always said borrow what you could pay on one wage. If I lost the police job in 2031, Connor's wage would need to cover it. That's just common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for, to know when to move to custody?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the force starts handing the planning and reports to the computer properly, not just trials. Once that happens, I'd ask the next week. I wouldn't wait for them to choose for me.

say: I'd say **look after your own** and keep officers on the streets.
I'd want **our priest** to address it from the pulpit.
think: Five years allows the **proper wedding** and a house first.
I'd want a **hands-on role** like custody by 2031.
do: Keep the **wedding** as planned next summer.
Buy a house in year two with a **smaller mortgage**.
Ask to move to **custody** around year three.
feel: She feels **anxious** but quieter, like a hard winter coming.
S3.quote: My mum always said borrow what you could pay on one wage.
fieldNote: Her mother's rule, **borrow on one wage**, guides her mortgage choice.
She'd move to **custody** as soon as the force adopts AI for real.
Faith and **community** remain her main frame for coping.

steps.text: Hold the wedding next summer as planned
Buy a house in year two on a mortgage one wage could cover
Ask to move to custody once the force adopts AI properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. That's a whole life, nearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone not to be ready, and families should plan for it like anything else. I'd say it after Mass and at Sunday dinner. I wouldn't be making a fuss about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I'd be married, with a house and maybe two kids, and ten years of experience before AGI. I'd still dread it, but I'd have time to find a corner of the job that stays human. Robots in 2039, I'd be 40. That's not young, but it's not old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep learning it properly. Connor and I would have the wedding, buy a house and start a family on our normal timeline. I'd learn the one AI tool I have to when it becomes compulsory. Around year five I'd look at custody or a schools liaison role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd get on with life. You can't stop living for something ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about having children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ten years is enough to raise them through primary school before anything happens. You don't put your family on hold for a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older people on my patch, honestly. If everything's run by AI, who checks on Mr Kelly when he falls, or spots the scam call before it empties his account? That's the part of policing I'd fight to keep.

say: I'd say families should **plan for it** like anything else.
I'd share this view **after Mass** and at Sunday dinner, without fuss.
think: I'd be married with a **house and maybe children** before AGI.
At **40** when robots arrive, I'd be neither young nor old.
do: Keep doing the job and **learning it properly**.
Have the wedding, house and **children** on our normal timeline.
Look at **custody or schools** liaison around year five.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but determined to get on with life.
S4.quote: You don't put your family on hold for a computer.
fieldNote: She refuses to put **family plans** on hold for technology.
Her strongest concern is for **older residents** who rely on officers.
Ten years lets her **resistance** coexist with normal life.

steps.text: Keep walking the Ashfield beat and learning the job properly
Marry Connor, buy a house and start a family on time
Look at custody or schools liaison roles around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the force keeping neighbourhood officers as people, by rule, and families and parishes looking out for each other. I don't expect much from the government, but I'd expect them not to make it worse.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the older people. Everyone's worried about jobs, and fair enough. But when every officer is busy with a computer or gone, who knocks on the old man's door to see if he's eaten?

headlineQuote: When every officer is busy with a computer or gone, who knocks on the old man's door to see if he's eaten?
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old** officer policing Ashfield, the old district where she grew up.
She's **traditional**, rooted in family, parish and her retired firefighter father's advice.
She **refuses AI tools**, wanting every word of her reports to be her own in court.
With a **wedding** and house ahead, faster AGI makes her scale back and lean on family.
Given **ten years** she keeps her plans and looks for a hands-on corner like custody.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when she expects juniors like her to be cut.
whatWouldHelp: Families and **parishes** looking out for each other.
